The Obesity Gene

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Scientists discover a malfunctioning gene is one of the causes of obesity

Summary:
Obesity has been seen as the result of too much food intake and too little exercise. However, scientists at MIT has discovered that the so-called obesity gene is also playing a major role in causing obesity. Some people's genetic make-up dictate that they will be fat and other's genes dictate that they will be thin. Scientists unravel this mystery.

Further information:
Scientists have discovered how a key gene related to obesity works when it is faulty - which could signal the future prevention and even cure the health problem.

Since 2007 scientists have known that a gene named FTO was related to obesity and people with higher BMIs (Body Mass Index) have been found to carry a variant of this gene. But despite this, it had not been known how or why FTO was related to obesity.

Now, researchers at MIT and Harvard Medical School believe they have discovered that a faulty version of this gene causes energy from food to become stored as fat in the body rather than be burned, contributing to obesity.


In the study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, scientists took cell samples from Europeans with either a healthy or faulty version of the FTO gene.

The findings showed that the faulty FTO gene ‘switched on’ two other genes – IRX3 and IRX5 – which have been identified as the “master controllers” of the process of thermogenesis as they can prevent the process in which energy is turned into heat, meaning it is instead stored as fat.

“Obesity has traditionally been seen as the result of an imbalance between the amount of food we eat and how much we exercise, but this view ignores the contribution of genetics to each individual’s metabolism,” senior author Manolis Kellis said.

Being overweight and obesity has been closely linked to 10 common cancers. Obesity has been identified as one of the biggest public health challenges of the 21st Century and already affects 500 million people worldwide. It has been credited with contributing to potentially fatal disorders such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and cancer.

But the discovery means there could be a cure on the way. “It’s a big deal,” Dr Clifford Rosen, a scientist at Maine Medical Centre Research Institute, and an associate editor of the medical journal told the Associated Press.

“A lot of people think the obesity epidemic is about eating too much,” but fat cells play a role in how food is used, he said.

He said the discovery means “you now have a pathway for drugs that can make those fat cells work differently.”

Press Release:


Obesity Genes
Could you perhaps have the so-called Obesity Gene variants that are linked to a higher body mass index and fat storage? This condition and its associated adverse health effects constitute the biggest public health challenges of this century and affect 500 million people worldwide. Carte Blanche asks - could new evidence around genes linked to obesity assist us in reversing both this global health crisis and our own ill health?


Script:


Manolis Kellis:
Obesity is a plague in our society. There is 600 million people worldwide who are affected by obesity and in the US alone it cost 2 billion dollars annually in the US healthcare system.
V/O:
Prof Manolis Kellis of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the USA is one of the world’s foremost researchers on obesity. He says obesity brings real health risks.
Manolis:
It impacts diseases across the entire human body. From the brain to the liver to the gut to the heart and every aspect of human biology is affected.
V/O:
Bronwyn Stokes, a dietician from Pretoria says obesity is also a massive problem here in South Africa.
Bronwyn:
They found that actually 40 percent of South African women are obese which means that their BMI is over 30. So obesity is a huge problem.
Derek:
And with children?
Bronwyn:
And with children. They say one in 5 girls and one 4 boys between the ages of 2 and 14 are either overweight or obese. So it’s become a big problem in school children, for sure.
Derek:
How do you and other dieticians go about treating obesity?
Bronwyn:
So we’ll look at their diet in relation to the exercise they do and we obviously look at their body composition as well. So we would look at strategies to help them improve their muscle mass and their body fat percentage. But at the moment it is still got to do with that balance between how much you eat and how much of that energy you use.
V/O:
And these treatment regimens have not changed much in a very long time.
Derek Link:
So, traditionally obesity was seen as the result of over-eating and a lack of exercise. But that thinking changed a few years ago.
V/O:
And it changed as a result of what scientists discovered when they started to investigate human DNA.
Manolis
Deep inside your cells lies a program that governs how that cell will work and how it will respond to changes in the environment to stimuli to signals that are coming to it. And that program sits inside the nucleus of every one of your cells.
V/O:
This program is your DNA. It is a string-like molecule and under an electron microscope it looks like this.

In a living cell it is arranged as a twisting double helix. This DNA strand contains the genetic code that determine who we are -- as individuals and as a species.
V/O:
Spread out across this strand are roughly 20 000 genes that code for proteins that regulate all the functions in our cells.

And these genes are themselves regulated by thousands of sets of instructions also located on or above the DNA strand known as the epigenome. These instructions determine the function or expression of the genes in the multitude of cell types in our bodies.
Manolis:
And that human epigenome is extremely dynamic from cell type to cell type. My brain cells are very different from my liver cells from my heart cells from my eyelids… because of epigenomics.
V/O:
But sometimes these instructions can go awry. Epigenetic errors can occur. This can lead to abnormal gene activity or gene inactivity or mutations. And many diseases are the result of epigenetic errors – some cancers and degenerative disorders have been linked to epigenetic errors.

While unravelling the mysteries of our DNA, in 2007, scientists discovered a new gene called the FTO gene. It was sensational as this gene could be linked to obesity.
Manolis:
Back then it was a complete and utter surprise. This gene that no one had actually heard of suddenly it became the focus a lot of investigation both in academic and in industry because of the huge implication of obesity on the economy of every country in the world.
LINK:
Scientists worldwide started to study the working of the so-called obesity gene intensely.
Manolis:
A lot of the central dogma surrounding obesity has centred on the brain. On one hand how much we eat and on the other how much we exercise. Calories in calories out. It has always been a very simple equation.
V/O:
It was believed that the brain was involved because it controlled appetite and exercise. The idea was that the FTO gene was linked to the brain.

However, no such link between the brain and obesity could be established.
LINK:
But Manolis, with his interest in epigenetics focused on the regulatory regions on the DNA string that was controlling this gene.
V/O:
Although Manolis also looked at brain cells, his team investigated 127 other cell types all over the body to see if they had any links to the FTO gene.
Manolis:
And what we found was quite striking. It was painting a very different picture. Basically it was telling us that instead of the brain this region was by far the most active in adipose, in the fat cells within our body, indicating a completely different mechanism might be at play rather than simply control of appetite or control of exercise.
V/O:
So they discovered that the brain had little to do with obesity, but that fat cells were involved. Then they made another discovery.
Manolis:
The data was pointing us to a switch, a master regulatory switch that sits inside our fat cells and decides if the excess calories in our bodies in the excess calories in our diet will be transformed to lipids and stored inside our fat cells for a rainy day or if they will be dissipated away as heat in a process known as thermogenesis or simply generation of heat.
V/O:
In most people this switch functions correctly and tell cells to store fat only when necessary. But in some people the epigenetic instructions regulating the switch in fat cells are faulty.
Manolis:
And what we found was that that switch was broken in the risk individuals with an increased probability of developing obesity. And that switch was stuck in the “store lipids” side of it. And for the rest of the individuals the non-risk individuals that switch was perfectly functioning and it go would back and forth between obese “store energy” or lean “burn energy” according to environmental cues.
V/O:
WThey also figured out that the faulty instruction, the mutation that caused the faulty switch involved more than just the FTO gene..
Manolis:
It was in fact two other genes that were sitting 1.2 million nucleotides away and 600 000 nucleotides away.
V/O:
A nucleotide is a basic DNA building block and many of them together make up the DNA string. So the newly discovered genes were found very far from the FTO gene site.
LINK
These genes were the IRX3 and IRX5 genes and they determined whether excess calories are stored as fat or dissipated as heat.
Manolis:
Once we had identified the circuitry, once we had a mechanism that we have hypothesised about how it was working that allowed us now to start manipulating that circuit. It allowed us to start intervening at the target genes IRX3 and IRX5 to alter their gene expression and their function to see what kind of effect this has on metabolism at the cellular level and the organism level.
V/O
With their knowledge of how the epigenome controls gene expression they knew how to change the instructions to the IRX3 and IRX5 genes so that the faulty fat cell switch could be repaired and the cells could start to function normally again. It came down to altering only a tiny piece of the DNA.
Manolis:
So suddenly you could restore a broken process by editing a single letter in the human genome. People talk a lot about precision medicine. I do not know how much more precise it gets than taking one letter out of 3.2 billion and saying if I change that letter, I am going to restore that process in that cell.
V/O:
Then they ran some tests on human cells in the lab and also experimented on mice.
Manolis:
Having understood that circuitry we could now switch human fat cells that store energy into cells that burn energy. We could change mice from obese to lean. A single modification in the human DNA could restore the functioning of that circuit. Changing the expression of a single gene in mice made them lose 50% of their body weight.
V/O:
It was a massive breakthrough, and for the first time the way genes contribute to obesity has been fully understood. The challenge now is to figure out a way to treat human subjects with the faulty switch.
Manolis:
If we can replicate these results in human, perhaps we have it in our hands the key to combating obesity.
LINK:
Manolis warns that treatments using this technique are still many years away. But would this breakthrough mean that in future we can eat what we like and not exercise?
Bronwyn:
By no means a quick fix. Diet and exercise are still going to be important in my opinion. you’re still going to have to watch what you eat and you’re still going to have to try to be as active as possible to ensure that you have the best body composition possible
Manolis:
We shouldn’t forget everything is intertwined and everything is interconnected in human biology. The genome is part of it, the environment is part of it and our own will is part of it.
